name: Alginic acid
text:
Alginic acid is a polysaccharide extracted from brown seaweed. It swells in water and is used as a thickener, stabiliser and gelling agent, and it can also help keep mixtures from separating.

It appears in desserts, puddings, jams and jellies, and some soups.

It is approved in the EU for jams and jellies, desserts and puddings, approved in the UK, and approved in the US in soups and soup mixes.

name: Sodium alginate
text:
Sodium alginate is the sodium salt of alginic acid, obtained from brown seaweed. It dissolves in water to form viscous solutions and forms gels in the presence of calcium.

It is used as a thickener, stabiliser and gelling agent in ice cream, sauces, desserts, restructured foods and fruit preparations, and in molecular gastronomy for forming gel spheres.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Potassium alginate
text:
Potassium alginate is the potassium salt of alginic acid, a polysaccharide extracted from brown seaweed. Like the other alginates, it thickens liquids and can form gels when calcium is present.

It is used as a thickener, stabiliser and gelling agent in desserts, sauces, dairy products and similar foods.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Ammonium alginate
text:
Ammonium alginate is the ammonium salt of alginic acid, which is obtained from brown seaweed. It is a water-soluble polysaccharide that increases viscosity.

It is used as a thickener and stabiliser in foods such as desserts, sauces and dairy-type products, although it is less common than sodium alginate.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Calcium alginate
text:
Calcium alginate is the calcium salt of alginic acid from brown seaweed. Unlike the sodium salt it does not dissolve in water, but it forms firm gels and films.

It is used as a thickener, stabiliser and gelling agent, for example in desserts, restructured meat and fruit products, and in sausage casings.

It is approved in the EU for jams and jellies, meat preparations, desserts and puddings, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Propylene glycol alginate
text:
Propylene glycol alginate (propane-1,2-diol alginate) is a semi-synthetic derivative of alginic acid, made by reacting seaweed alginate with propylene oxide. It is stable in acidic liquids, where plain alginates tend to precipitate.

It is used as a thickener, stabiliser and emulsifier, notably in salad dressings, sauces, acidic drinks and beer foam stabilisation.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, approved in the UK, and approved in the US with conditions.

name: Agar
text:
Agar is a gelling substance extracted from red seaweeds. It dissolves in hot water and sets into a firm gel on cooling, and it is widely used as a plant-based alternative to gelatin.

It is used in jellies, desserts, confectionery, dairy products and bakery fillings, and also in microbiology media.

It is approved in the EU for jams and jellies, tablets and fermented creams, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Carrageenan
text:
Carrageenan is a group of polysaccharides extracted from red seaweeds. It thickens and gels liquids and reacts with milk proteins to stabilise them.

It is used in dairy products, chocolate milk, ice cream, desserts, processed meats and plant-based milks.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, approved in the UK, and approved in the US. Some people have raised concerns about degraded carrageenan, but regulators have approved the food-grade form.

name: Processed eucheuma seaweed
text:
Processed eucheuma seaweed is made by washing and treating red seaweed of the Eucheuma family without extracting the carrageenan, so it keeps some of the seaweed's other components. It is a less refined relative of carrageenan.

It is used as a thickener, stabiliser and gelling agent, mainly in meat products.

It is approved in the EU for meat preparations only, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Baker's yeast glycan
text:
Baker's yeast glycan is a polysaccharide fraction obtained from the cell walls of baker's yeast. It is a rarely used additive with an emulsifying function.

In the US it may be used in salad dressing, frozen yogurt, sour cream, cheese spread and their analogs.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK, and it is approved in the US for the products listed above.

name: Arabinogalactan
text:
Arabinogalactan is a complex polysaccharide of plant origin, commonly obtained from larch wood. It dissolves easily in water and has low viscosity.

It is a little-used additive, generally used as a stabiliser or binder, and also appears in some dietary fibre supplements.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK, and it is approved in the US.

name: Locust bean gum
text:
Locust bean gum, also called carob gum, is a polysaccharide extracted from the seeds of the carob tree. It thickens cold and hot liquids and gels in combination with xanthan or carrageenan.

It is used in ice cream, dairy desserts, cream cheese, sauces and bakery fillings, and as a stabiliser and emulsifier.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Oat gum
text:
Oat gum is a soluble fibre extract from oats, composed mainly of beta-glucans. It is a rarely used thickener and stabiliser.

Where it is allowed, it may be added to foods to increase viscosity and improve texture.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK, and it is approved in the US.

name: Guar gum
text:
Guar gum is a polysaccharide obtained from the seeds of the guar plant, grown mainly in India and Pakistan. It thickens cold liquids very efficiently.

It is used as a thickener and stabiliser in sauces, dressings, ice cream, bakery products, dairy products and gluten-free baking.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, approved in the UK, and approved in the US. Contamination of guar gum with dioxin led to a recall in the EU in 2007.

name: Tragacanth
text:
Tragacanth is a natural gum obtained from the dried sap of Astragalus shrubs growing in the Middle East. It is one of the oldest gums used by humans and gives viscous, acid-stable solutions.

It is used as a thickener, stabiliser and emulsifier in dressings, sauces, confectionery and icings.

It is approved in the EU in sweeteners and meat preparations, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Gum arabic
text:
Gum arabic, also called acacia gum, is the dried sap of Acacia trees, mainly from the Sahel region of Africa. It dissolves easily in water and is a very effective stabiliser.

It is used in soft drinks and drink emulsions, confectionery such as gum drops and pastilles, and in glazes and flavour encapsulation.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, approved in the UK, and approved in the US with conditions.

name: Xanthan gum
text:
Xanthan gum is a polysaccharide produced by fermenting sugars with the bacterium Xanthomonas campestris. It gives high viscosity at low concentrations and is stable to heat and acid.

It is used as a thickener and stabiliser in sauces, dressings, gluten-free baked goods, dairy products and drinks.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, approved in the UK, and approved in the US. In large amounts it can have a laxative effect.

name: Karaya gum
text:
Karaya gum is a natural gum obtained from the sap of the Sterculia urens tree, native to India. It swells strongly in water and forms viscous dispersions.

It is used as a thickener, stabiliser and emulsifier in small quantities, for example in some desserts and bakery products, and it is also used in denture adhesives.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Tara gum
text:
Tara gum is a polysaccharide extracted from the seeds of the tara shrub, grown mainly in Peru. Its thickening power lies between that of guar gum and locust bean gum.

It is used as a thickener and stabiliser in dairy products, ice cream, sauces and similar foods.

It is approved in the EU and the UK, and not approved in the US.

name: Gellan gum
text:
Gellan gum is a polysaccharide produced by fermentation with the bacterium Sphingomonas elodea. It forms clear, heat-stable gels at very low concentrations.

It is used as a gelling agent, thickener and stabiliser in jellies, fruit preparations, dairy and plant-based drinks, where it keeps particles suspended.

It is approved in the EU in jams, jellies and sweeteners, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Gum ghatti
text:
Gum ghatti is a natural gum obtained from the sap of the Anogeissus latifolia tree, which grows in India and Sri Lanka. It works as an emulsifier and stabiliser, somewhat like gum arabic.

It is used in some beverage emulsions and similar products where it is permitted.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK, and it is approved in the US.

name: Sorbitol
text:
Sorbitol is a sugar alcohol (polyol) made industrially by hydrogenating glucose; it also occurs naturally in some fruits. It is about half as sweet as sugar and has fewer calories per gram.

It is used as a sweetener, humectant (to keep foods moist) and bulking agent in sugar-free sweets, chewing gum, baked goods and diabetic products.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, approved in the UK, and approved in the US with conditions. In large amounts it can have a laxative effect, and the EU requires a warning on products that could cause this.

name: Mannitol
text:
Mannitol is a sugar alcohol found naturally in seaweed, mushrooms and some plants, and also produced industrially by hydrogenating sugars. It is about half as sweet as sugar and does not absorb moisture easily.

It is used as a sweetener and anti-caking agent, for example as a dusting powder on chewing gum and in sugar-free confectionery.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, approved in the UK, and approved in the US with conditions. Large amounts can have a laxative effect.

name: Glycerol
text:
Glycerol (glycerine) is a clear, sweet-tasting syrupy liquid. It is a by-product of fat and oil processing and can also be made from plant oils or synthetically.

In food it is used as a humectant, solvent and sweetener, and it keeps products such as cakes, icings, confectionery and soft cookies moist.

It is approved in the EU in sweeteners and cocoa products, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Octenyl succinic acid modified gum arabic
text:
This additive is gum arabic that has been chemically modified with octenyl succinic acid, which makes it a better emulsifier than plain gum arabic, especially for oil-in-water emulsions.

It is used to stabilise flavour emulsions in drinks, sauces and icings.

It is approved in the EU in icing, sauces and certain flavoured drinks, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Curdlan
text:
Curdlan is a polysaccharide made by fermentation with the bacterium Agrobacterium (Alcaligenes faecalis). On heating in water it forms firm, heat-stable gels.

It is used as a gelling agent, mainly in noodles, tofu-like products and processed meat and fish products, especially in Asian cuisine.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, not approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Konjac
text:
Konjac is obtained from the tuber of the konjac plant (Amorphophallus konjac) and consists mainly of glucomannan, a soluble dietary fibre. It forms very viscous solutions and elastic gels.

It is used as a thickener and gelling agent and in Asian noodles and jellies. Konjac jelly sweets in mini-cup form have caused choking deaths, so they are banned in the EU.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, approved in the UK, and not approved in the US.

name: Soybean hemicellulose
text:
Soybean hemicellulose is a water-soluble polysaccharide extracted from the fibre of soybeans. It works as a stabiliser and emulsifier, particularly in acidic drinks that contain protein.

It is approved in the EU in jelly, frozen egg products and liquid food supplements, and it is not approved in the UK. In the US, soybean is approved, but hemicellulose has no specific record in the FDA database.

name: Cassia gum
text:
Cassia gum is a galactomannan polysaccharide extracted from the seeds of Cassia tora and Cassia obtusifolia. It thickens and stabilises liquids, and it forms gels together with other gums such as xanthan.

It is used in processed cheese, dairy desserts, ice cream and some pet foods.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, approved in the UK, and not approved in the US.

name: Gelatin
text:
Gelatin is a protein obtained by partial hydrolysis of collagen from the skin and bones of animals, usually pigs and cattle. It dissolves in hot water and sets into a clear gel when cooled.

It is used in jellies, gummy sweets, marshmallows, desserts, yogurts and capsules. It is not suitable for vegetarians or for those following halal or kosher rules in some cases.

It is not listed in the EU and UK as it is not considered an additive, and it is approved in the US.

name: Peptones
text:
Peptones are mixtures of short protein fragments produced by breaking down animal or plant proteins with enzymes or acids. Their main use is as nutrient components in culture media.

They are not approved in the EU or the UK, and they are approved in the US.

name: Polyoxyethylene (8) stearate
text:
Polyoxyethylene (8) stearate is a synthetic emulsifier made by combining stearic acid with polyethylene glycol. It was formerly used in bakery products to keep them soft.

It is not approved in the EU, UK or US, so it is not in current use in those regions.

name: Polyoxyethylene (40) stearate
text:
Polyoxyethylene (40) stearate is a synthetic emulsifier made from stearic acid and polyethylene glycol. It has historically been used to improve the texture of bakery goods.

It is approved in the EU, not approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Polysorbate 20
text:
Polysorbate 20 (polyoxyethylene sorbitan monolaurate) is a synthetic emulsifier made from sorbitol, lauric acid and ethylene oxide. It helps oil and water mix and disperses flavours.

It is used in small amounts in sauces, dressings, desserts, flavour preparations and some drinks.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, approved in the UK, and approved in the US with conditions.

name: Polysorbate 80
text:
Polysorbate 80 (polyoxyethylene sorbitan mono-oleate) is a synthetic emulsifier made from sorbitol, oleic acid and ethylene oxide. It stabilises mixtures of oil and water.

It is used in ice cream, sauces, dressings, desserts and vitamin and flavour preparations, and also in pharmaceuticals and cosmetics.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, approved in the UK, and approved in the US with conditions.

name: Polysorbate 40
text:
Polysorbate 40 (polyoxyethylene sorbitan monopalmitate) is a synthetic emulsifier made from sorbitol, palmitic acid and ethylene oxide. It is used to mix oil and water and to stabilise foams and emulsions.

It is used in small amounts in bakery fillings, whipped toppings, desserts and similar products.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, approved in the UK, and approved in the US with conditions.

name: Polysorbate 60
text:
Polysorbate 60 (polyoxyethylene sorbitan monostearate) is a synthetic emulsifier made from sorbitol, stearic acid and ethylene oxide. It helps oil and water stay mixed and improves the texture of fatty foods.

It is used in whipped toppings, cake mixes, icings, dressings and ice cream.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, approved in the UK, and approved in the US with conditions.

name: Polysorbate 65
text:
Polysorbate 65 (polyoxyethylene sorbitan tristearate) is a synthetic emulsifier made from sorbitol, stearic acid and ethylene oxide. It stabilises emulsions and foams.

It is used in small amounts in ice cream, desserts and whipped toppings.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Pectin
text:
Pectin is a polysaccharide found in the cell walls of fruit and extracted commercially, mostly from citrus peel and apple pomace. Amidated pectin is a modified form with improved gelling in some conditions.

It is the classic gelling agent for jams and marmalades, and it is also used as a thickener and stabiliser in fruit fillings, confectionery and dairy desserts.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Gelatine
text:
Gelatine is a protein obtained by partial hydrolysis of animal collagen, mainly from pig skin, cattle hides and bones. It forms a clear gel when its hot solution is cooled.

It is used in jellies, gummy sweets, marshmallows, desserts and dairy products. It is of animal origin, so it is unsuitable for vegetarians and vegans.

It is not listed in the EU and UK as it is not considered an additive, and it is approved in the US.

name: Ammonium phosphatides
text:
Ammonium phosphatides are emulsifiers made from glycerol, fatty acids and phosphoric acid, with ammonium salts of phosphated fatty acids; they are produced synthetically from vegetable oils, often rapeseed oil.

They are used mainly in chocolate and cocoa products, where they reduce viscosity.

They are approved in the EU in cocoa and chocolate products only, approved in the UK, and not approved in the US.

name: Brominated vegetable oil
text:
Brominated vegetable oil is a vegetable oil chemically modified with bromine. It was used in some citrus-flavoured soft drinks to keep flavour oils evenly dispersed.

Bromine can accumulate in the body, and the use of the additive was restricted or withdrawn in several countries.

It is not approved in the EU, UK or US.

name: Sucrose acetate isobutyrate
text:
Sucrose acetate isobutyrate is a synthetic, thick, honey-like substance made from sucrose, acetic acid and isobutyric acid. It is very dense and is used to keep flavour oils from floating in drinks.

It is used in cloudy beverages.

It is approved in the EU for certain cloudy beverages, approved in the UK, and approved in the US for non-alcoholic beverages.

name: Glycerol esters of wood rosins
text:
Glycerol esters of wood rosins, also called ester gum, are made by reacting glycerol with resin acids from pine wood. They are dense substances that help keep flavour oils evenly distributed in drinks.

They are used in cloudy drinks and as a coating on citrus fruit.

They are approved in the EU for certain cloudy beverages and surface treatment of citrus fruit, approved in the UK, and approved in the US for certain beverages.

name: Succistearin
text:
Succistearin, also known as stearoyl propylene glycol hydrogen succinate, is a synthetic emulsifier related to fatty acid esters. It is little used.

It can be added to cakes, pastries, fillings and toppings in the US.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK, and it is approved in the US for cakes, pastries, filling and toppings.

name: Diphosphates
text:
Diphosphates (pyrophosphates) are sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium salts of diphosphoric acid. They are made industrially from phosphoric acid and the corresponding mineral compounds.

They are used as emulsifiers, raising agents and stabilisers, for example in baking powder, processed cheese, processed meat, and as a way to prevent discolouration of potatoes.

They are approved in the EU with conditions and approved in the UK. In the US, approval covers the forms numbered i, iii, iv, v and vi. Because they add phosphorus to the diet, total phosphate intake is regulated.

name: Triphosphates
text:
Triphosphates are sodium and potassium salts of triphosphoric acid: sodium triphosphate (pentasodium triphosphate) and pentapotassium triphosphate. They are made industrially from phosphoric acid.

They hold water in meat and fish, stabilise emulsions and act as sequestrants in processed foods.

They are approved in the EU in certain fish products, approved in the UK, and approved in the US. Phosphate additives add to total dietary phosphorus intake.

name: Polyphosphates
text:
Polyphosphates are salts of long-chain phosphoric acids: sodium, potassium, sodium calcium, calcium and ammonium polyphosphates. They are made industrially from phosphoric acid.

They bind water and metals, so they are used in processed meat, fish products, processed cheese and some drinks as emulsifiers and stabilisers.

They are approved in the EU in certain fish products, approved in the UK, and approved in the US for the sodium and potassium forms (i and ii).

name: Beta-cyclodextrin
text:
Beta-cyclodextrin is a ring-shaped oligosaccharide of seven glucose units, made enzymatically from starch. Its ring can enclose small molecules such as flavours and vitamins.

It is used to bind flavours, to stabilise them in powders, and as a carrier or binder in tablets.

It is approved in the EU for flavoured powdered instant drinks and foods in tablet form, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Cellulose
text:
Cellulose is the main structural component of plant cell walls and is obtained mostly from wood pulp or cotton. Microcrystalline cellulose is a purified, partly broken-down form; powdered cellulose is a finely ground form.

Both are indigestible fibre and are used as bulking agents, anti-caking agents and texture improvers in grated cheese, low-fat products, baked goods and tablets.

It is approved in the EU with conditions, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Methyl cellulose
text:
Methyl cellulose is made by chemically modifying cellulose with methyl groups. It dissolves in cold water and, unusually, forms a gel when heated.

It is used as a thickener, emulsifier and binder in vegetarian meat substitutes, batters, sauces and gluten-free baking. It is not digested and acts like dietary fibre.

It is approved in the EU in sweeteners, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Ethyl cellulose
text:
Ethyl cellulose is a cellulose derivative made by treating cellulose with ethyl groups. It is insoluble in water but dissolves in some organic solvents, and it forms films.

It is used as a binder and filler in tablets and as a coating or encapsulation material.

It is approved in the EU, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Hydroxypropyl cellulose
text:
Hydroxypropyl cellulose is a cellulose derivative made by treating cellulose with propylene oxide. It dissolves in water and many solvents and forms films.

It is used as an emulsifier, thickener and stabiliser, for example in whipped toppings and in tablets and coatings.

It is approved in the EU in sweeteners, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Low-substituted hydroxypropyl cellulose
text:
Low-substituted hydroxypropyl cellulose (L-HPC) is a cellulose derivative with a small amount of hydroxypropyl groups. It is insoluble in water but swells strongly, which makes it useful as a tablet disintegrant and binder.

It is approved in the EU, approved in the UK, and not approved in the US.

name: Hypromellose
text:
Hypromellose (hydroxypropyl methylcellulose) is a cellulose derivative made by treating cellulose with methyl chloride and propylene oxide. It dissolves in water and forms films and gels.

It is used as a thickener, emulsifier and film former, in vegetarian capsules, coatings, sauces and gluten-free baking.

It is approved in the EU in sweeteners, citrus fruit, melons and pomegranates, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Ethyl methyl cellulose
text:
Ethyl methyl cellulose is a cellulose derivative carrying both ethyl and methyl groups. It is used as a foaming agent, emulsifier and stabiliser, for example in whipped products.

It is approved in the EU in sweeteners, approved in the UK, and not approved in the US.

name: Carboxymethyl cellulose
text:
Carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC, cellulose gum) is made by treating cellulose with chloroacetic acid. Its sodium salt dissolves in water to form clear, viscous solutions.

It is used as a thickener and stabiliser in ice cream, sauces, dressings, drinks, low-fat foods and baked goods.

It is approved in the EU with conditions and approved in the UK. It is not approved in the US.

name: Ethyl hydroxyethyl cellulose
text:
Ethyl hydroxyethyl cellulose is a cellulose ether, a chemically modified form of cellulose. It is mainly known for industrial uses such as paints and adhesives.

It is not approved in the EU, UK or US.

name: Croscarmellose
text:
Croscarmellose is cross-linked sodium carboxymethyl cellulose. It does not dissolve in water but swells strongly, which is why it is mainly used as a disintegrant in tablets and food supplements.

It is approved in the EU for sweeteners and supplements, and the additive is under discussion for a future amendment of the EU directive. It is approved in the UK and not approved in the US.

name: Enzymically hydrolysed carboxymethylcellulose
text:
Enzymically hydrolysed carboxymethylcellulose is carboxymethyl cellulose that has been partly broken down by enzymes, giving a lower-viscosity product that works as a source of soluble fibre and stabiliser.

It is approved in the EU, approved in the UK, and not approved in the US.

name: Salts of fatty acids (sodium, potassium, calcium)
text:
These are the sodium, potassium and calcium salts of edible fatty acids, which are essentially soaps made from food fats. They are made by treating fats or fatty acids with the corresponding alkali.

They are used as emulsifiers and anti-caking agents, for example to keep powders free-flowing.

They are approved in the EU for sweeteners and dried herbs and spices, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Magnesium salts of fatty acids
text:
Magnesium salts of fatty acids, such as magnesium stearate, are made by combining edible fatty acids with magnesium. They are fine powders that repel water.

They are used as anti-caking agents and emulsifiers, and widely as a lubricant in making tablets.

They are approved in the EU for sweeteners, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids
text:
Mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids are esters of glycerol and fatty acids, made from vegetable oils or animal fats. They are among the most widely used emulsifiers.

They are used in bread, cakes, margarine, ice cream, sweets, and spreads to improve texture and keep products soft. The source can be plant or animal, which matters to vegetarians.

They are approved in the EU for certain foods, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Acetic acid esters of mono- and diglycerides
text:
This emulsifier is made by reacting mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids with acetic acid. It helps whip and stabilise fat-containing foods.

It is used in whipped toppings, baked goods, and coatings for fruit.

It is approved in the EU for certain foods, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Lactic acid esters of mono- and diglycerides
text:
This emulsifier is made by reacting mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids with lactic acid. It improves aeration and stability.

It is used in whipped toppings, baked goods and baby food.

It is approved in the EU for biscuits and rusks, cereal-based foods and baby foods, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Citric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides
text:
This emulsifier is made by reacting mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids with citric acid. It blends well with both fats and water.

It is used in margarine, bakery products, sauces, infant formula and processed meats.

It is approved in the EU for certain foods, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Tartaric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides
text:
This emulsifier is made by reacting mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids with tartaric acid. It is rarely used on its own.

It can improve dough in bread-making.

It is approved in the EU for bread, approved in the UK, and not approved in the US.

name: Diacetyl tartaric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides
text:
This emulsifier, often abbreviated DATEM, is made by reacting mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids with diacetyl tartaric acid. It strengthens dough and increases bread volume.

It is used in bread, rolls and other yeast-raised baked goods.

It is approved in the EU for bread, approved in the UK, and not approved in the US.

name: Mixed acetic and tartaric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides
text:
This emulsifier is made by reacting mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids with a mixture of acetic and tartaric acids. It is used as a dough conditioner.

It is approved in the EU for bread, approved in the UK, and not approved in the US.

name: Succinylated monoglycerides
text:
Succinylated monoglycerides are made by reacting monoglycerides of fatty acids with succinic acid. They are dough strengtheners that improve bread volume and texture.

They are not approved in the EU or the UK, and they are approved in the US in bread.

name: Sucrose esters of fatty acids
text:
Sucrose esters of fatty acids are made by combining sugar with fatty acids from edible oils. Depending on the composition, they can emulsify oil in water or the reverse.

They are used in baked goods, confectionery, ice cream, drinks and dairy desserts, and as coatings for fruit.

They are approved in the EU for certain foods, approved in the UK, and approved in the US for certain foods.

name: Sucroglycerides
text:
Sucroglycerides are mixtures of sucrose esters and mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids, made by reacting sugar with fats or oils. They are emulsifiers.

They are used in a range of foods such as baked goods and confectionery.

They are approved in the EU for certain foods, approved in the UK, and not approved in the US.

name: Polyglycerol esters of fatty acids
text:
Polyglycerol esters of fatty acids are made by combining polymerised glycerol with fatty acids from edible oils. They are versatile emulsifiers.

They are used in cakes, whipped toppings, margarine, confectionery and ice cream to stabilise emulsions and foams.

They are approved in the EU for certain foods, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Polyglycerol polyricinoleate
text:
Polyglycerol polyricinoleate (PGPR) is an emulsifier made from polyglycerol and castor oil fatty acids. It strongly reduces the viscosity of molten chocolate.

It is used in chocolate, chocolate coatings, spreads and low-fat spreads, which lets manufacturers use less cocoa butter.

It is approved in the EU for certain foods, approved in the UK, and not approved in the US.

name: Propylene glycol esters of fatty acids
text:
Propylene glycol esters of fatty acids (propane-1,2-diol esters) are made by reacting propylene glycol with fatty acids from edible oils. They are emulsifiers, often used to stabilise aerated foods.

They are used in cake mixes, whipped toppings and dessert products.

They are approved in the EU for certain foods, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Lactylated fatty acid esters of glycerol and propane-1,2-diol
text:
This emulsifier is made by reacting glycerol and propylene glycol (propane-1,2-diol) with fatty acids and lactic acid. It is used to stabilise foams and emulsions.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK, and it is approved in the US.

name: Thermally oxidized soya bean oil with mono- and diglycerides
text:
This emulsifier is made by heating soya bean oil in air and then reacting it with mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids. It helps prevent fat from spattering when food is fried.

It is used in fat emulsions such as frying margarine.

It is approved in the EU for fat emulsions only, approved in the UK, and not approved in the US.

name: Dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate
text:
Dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate (docusate sodium) is a synthetic surfactant. It is also well known as a stool-softening laxative in medicine, and it is used as a wetting agent in some foods.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK, and it is approved in the US.

name: Sodium stearoyl-2-lactylate
text:
Sodium stearoyl-2-lactylate is made from stearic acid and lactic acid, neutralised with sodium. It strengthens dough and improves the softness and volume of baked goods.

It is used in bread, cakes, dried potato products, sauces and creamers.

It is approved in the EU for certain foods, approved in the UK, and approved in the US for certain foods.

name: Calcium stearoyl-2-lactylate
text:
Calcium stearoyl-2-lactylate is made from stearic acid and lactic acid, neutralised with calcium. It works as a dough conditioner and emulsifier, similar to the sodium salt.

It is used in bread, bakery products, whipped toppings and creamers.

It is approved in the EU for certain foods, approved in the UK, and approved in the US for certain foods.

name: Stearyl tartrate
text:
Stearyl tartrate is an ester of stearyl alcohol and tartaric acid. It is a little-used emulsifier and dough conditioner.

It is approved in the EU, approved in the UK, and not approved in the US.

name: Stearyl citrate
text:
Stearyl citrate is an ester of stearyl alcohol and citric acid. It is a little-used emulsifier that can also bind traces of metals.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK, and it is approved in the US for certain foods.

name: Sodium stearoyl fumarate
text:
Sodium stearoyl fumarate is a synthetic emulsifier made from stearic acid and fumaric acid. It has been used as a dough conditioner.

It is not approved in the EU, UK or US.

name: Calcium stearoyl fumarate
text:
Calcium stearoyl fumarate is a synthetic emulsifier made from stearic acid and fumaric acid, the calcium counterpart of E485.

It is not approved in the EU, UK or US.

name: Sodium laurylsulfate
text:
Sodium laurylsulfate (sodium lauryl sulfate) is a synthetic surfactant, better known as a detergent in toothpaste and shampoos. In food it has been used as a whipping and foaming agent, for example in egg whites.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK, and it is approved in the US.

name: Ethoxylated mono- and diglycerides
text:
Ethoxylated mono- and diglycerides (polyglycerate 60) are emulsifiers made by reacting mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids with ethylene oxide. They help fat and water mix.

They are not approved in the EU or the UK, and they are approved in the US for certain foods.

name: Methyl glucoside-coconut oil ester
text:
Methyl glucoside-coconut oil ester is an emulsifier made from sugar-derived methyl glucoside and coconut oil fatty acids. It is a little-used additive.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK, and it is approved in the US for molasses and dextrose or sucrose.

name: Propane-1,2-diol
text:
Propane-1,2-diol, better known as propylene glycol, is a clear, colourless, slightly sweet liquid made synthetically from petroleum-derived propylene oxide. It mixes with water and many solvents.

It is used as a solvent for flavours and colours and as a humectant. It is not the same as the toxic ethylene glycol.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK, and it is approved in the US for certain foods.

name: Sorbitan monostearate
text:
Sorbitan monostearate is an emulsifier made by combining sorbitol with stearic acid. It helps oil and water mix and keeps fats evenly dispersed.

It is used in cakes, whipped toppings, chocolate, dry yeast and some fat-containing foods.

It is approved in the EU for certain foods, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Sorbitan tristearate
text:
Sorbitan tristearate is an emulsifier made by combining sorbitol with stearic acid. It is used to control crystallisation of fats and to stabilise emulsions.

It can be found in chocolate and fat-based products.

It is approved in the EU for certain foods, approved in the UK, and not approved in the US.

name: Sorbitan monolaurate
text:
Sorbitan monolaurate is an emulsifier made by combining sorbitol with lauric acid. It helps oil and water stay mixed.

It is used in small amounts in baked goods, whipped toppings and similar products.

It is approved in the EU for certain foods, approved in the UK, and not approved in the US.

name: Sorbitan monooleate
text:
Sorbitan monooleate is an emulsifier made by combining sorbitol with oleic acid. It is oil-soluble and used to stabilise emulsions.

It is used in small amounts in desserts, whipped products and vitamin preparations.

It is approved in the EU for certain foods, approved in the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Sorbitan monopalmitate
text:
Sorbitan monopalmitate is an emulsifier made by combining sorbitol with palmitic acid. It is used to disperse fats and stabilise emulsions.

It is approved in the EU for certain foods, approved in the UK, and not approved in the US.

name: Sorbitan trioleate
text:
Sorbitan trioleate is an emulsifier made by combining sorbitol with oleic acid. It is one of the less common sorbitan esters.

It is not approved in the EU, UK or US.

name: Polyoxypropylene-polyoxyethylene polymers
text:
These are synthetic block polymers of propylene oxide and ethylene oxide, which act as surfactants. They are sometimes called poloxamers.

They are not approved in the EU or the UK, and they are approved in the US.

name: Partial polyglycerol esters of polycondensed fatty acids of castor oil
text:
These are emulsifiers made from polyglycerol and fatty acids from castor oil that have been polymerised. They are closely related to polyglycerol polyricinoleate (E476).

They are not approved in the EU, UK or US.

name: Stigmasterol-rich plant sterols
text:
Stigmasterol-rich plant sterols are mixtures of sterols extracted from plants, containing a high proportion of stigmasterol. They are used in foods as a stabiliser or emulsifier-type additive.

They are approved in the EU for ready-to-freeze alcoholic cocktails, approved in the UK, and not approved in the US.
